newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says no date for N.Korea nuclear inspection.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says no date for N.Korea nuclear inspection.

text.p: Taiwan atomic energy regulators said on Monday they must first visit North Korea before approving a controversial plan to ship nuclear waste to the reclusive Stalinist state and no date for an inspection has been set.
"We need to complete our review of the documentation before we can schedule such a visit," an official of the Atomic Energy Council told Reuters.
"We are still sorting out three relevant documents submitted by Taiwan Power Co (Taipower)," he said.

The official said the council must see Korean import permits that are validated by Taiwan's government, details about vessels that will ship the waste and a North Korean operating permit for the waste dump before a trip can be scheduled.

Council members and Taipower executives had said they hoped to visit Pyongyang in July to inspect the site where the company proposes storing up to 200,000 barrels of low-level waste from state-run Taipower, which is running out of storage space.

The council denied a Taipei newspaper's weekend report that it had approved the deal, saying no approval was possible before a Pyongyang visit was completed and the dump site at Pingshan certified by both sides as safe.
It was not immediately known how much work needs to be done at Pingshan before it can be certified.

Under a contract signed between North Korea and Taipower in January, Pyongyang would provide a 4.8-sq-km (1.85-sq-mile) site to store the waste, with no one allowed to live within a five-km (three-mile) radius, council officials have said.

Financial details have not been disclosed, but unconfirmed reports say the deal could mean US$230 million to North Korea, which is starved for cash and reported to be on the brink of widespread famine due to floods and agricultural mismanagement.

South Korea, the Stalinist north's bitter rival since the Korean war, has strongly opposed Taipower's plan, saying it feared nuclear pollution and related health hazards on both sides of the divided Korean peninsula.

The deal also has been actively opposed by anti-nuclear activists in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, who say North Korea cannot be trusted with the waste and is accepting it only out of financial desperation.

International environmental group Greenpeace has added its support to the opponents, saying its own covert inspection of Taipower's main nuclear dump found some higher-level waste among that which the utility rated as low-level.
Taipower has three nuclear power stations in operation and has a fourth under construction.

Taipower's main waste dump on Lanyu island southeast of Taiwan, whose 98,112-barrel capacity is nearly full, must be cleared and closed by 2002 under an agreement made with local residents who oppose its presence there.
